passages.title: LITERARY NARRATIVE: "What Ready Looks Like" (an original story written for this practice set)
passages.text:
The bakery on Linden Street opened at six, but the work began at midnight. That was the first thing Mrs. Dalca told me when she hired me, the summer I was seventeen, and she said it the way other people mention the weather: a fact to be dressed for, not complained about. I nodded as if midnight were nothing. I had stayed up later than that for worse reasons.

The first week, I was useless in a way I had not known was possible. I measured flour too quickly and scattered it across the counter. I kneaded the dough as if it had insulted me. When the loaves came out of the oven flat and pale, Mrs. Dalca did not scold me. She broke one open, pressed the crumb between her fingers, and handed me half. "Taste what hurry tastes like," she said.

It tasted like nothing. That was the problem.

I wanted to be good at things immediately. At school I had been the kind of student who finished tests first and then waited, tapping a pencil, for everyone else. Speed had always looked like intelligence to me, and slowness like a kind of failure. The bakery did not care what I thought. Dough rose on its own schedule, and no amount of glaring at the proofing baskets made it rise faster.

Mrs. Dalca worked without a clock. She would lift the cloth from a bowl, press a floured finger into the dough, and watch the dent. If it sprang back at once, she covered the bowl again. If it filled in slowly, halfway, she nodded and reached for the scale. I asked her once how she knew how long to wait. She shrugged. "I don't know how long," she said. "I know what ready looks like."

By July I had stopped looking at the wall clock above the ovens. I began to notice other things instead: the sour, almost fruity smell that meant the starter was strong; the way a well-shaped loaf held its seam on the counter; the faint crackle, like distant rain, that came from the crusts as they cooled. None of these were things I could have learned faster by trying harder. They arrived when they arrived, the way the dough did.

On my last night, Mrs. Dalca let me make the rye on my own. I mixed and folded and waited, and when the loaves came out I broke one open the way she had that first week. The crumb was dark and open and smelled of caraway. I handed her half. She chewed for a long time, longer than seemed necessary, and I felt the old impatience rise in my chest. Then she nodded once, the same small nod she gave the dough.

"Now," she said, "it tastes like time."

passages.title: SOCIAL SCIENCE: Passage A is from an essay by an urban ecologist; Passage B is from an essay by a city planner. Both are original texts written for this practice set.
passages.text:
Passage A

For much of the last century, cities treated small streams as problems to be solved. A creek that flooded a neighborhood or carried away sewage was straightened, lined with concrete, and eventually sealed inside a pipe beneath the street. Out of sight, the stream stopped being anyone's concern.

In recent decades, a number of cities have begun to reverse that choice by "daylighting" buried streams: removing the pavement above them and rebuilding a channel open to the sky. Supporters often lead with the ecological case. An open channel, lined with gravel and shaded by plants, can support insects, fish, and birds that a dark pipe cannot. Exposed water also cools the air around it on hot days.

But the most persuasive argument may be the practical one. A pipe has a fixed capacity; when a storm sends more water than it can carry, the excess backs up into basements and streets. A restored stream with a wide, shallow floodplain can spread that water out and slow it down. In this sense, daylighting does not merely decorate a city; it gives the city room to absorb storms that pipes were never built for.

Daylighting is not cheap, and it is not always possible. Where buildings now sit directly above an old stream, the cost of restoration can be prohibitive. Yet the cities that have tried it often report a benefit no engineer predicted: people come. They walk along the water at lunch, bring children to look for minnows, and begin to treat the neighborhood as a place worth caring for. A stream that was once a problem to be hidden becomes, in a sense, a public room.

Passage B

Proposals to daylight buried streams are easy to love. Few people object to the image of clear water running where there was once only asphalt. As a city planner, though, I have learned to ask what such projects cost and what else the same money might do.

The answer is often sobering. Opening a stream through a dense neighborhood can mean acquiring property, rerouting utility lines, and rebuilding streets, work that may cost many times as much as repairing the existing pipe. For the same budget, a city might install rain gardens and permeable pavement across dozens of blocks, capturing storm water closer to where it falls.

Nor is a restored stream automatically a healthy one. Water that runs off city streets carries oil, salt, and litter. Unless the surrounding area is also changed, a daylighted stream may simply put polluted water on display. Some restored channels require years of maintenance before they support the wildlife their designers promised.

None of this means daylighting is never worth doing. Where a buried stream runs beneath an open lot or a park, the costs can be modest and the benefits real. My concern is with treating daylighting as a symbol rather than a tool. A city's first question should not be "How do we bring the stream back?" but "What is the most effective way to manage this water?" Sometimes the answer will be a stream. Often it will not.

questions.stem: The passage is primarily concerned with:

choices.A: a narrator's gradual shift from valuing speed to valuing patience, learned through work at a bakery.
choices.B: a teenager's struggle to balance schoolwork with a demanding night job.
choices.C: the history of a small family bakery and the people who run it.
choices.D: a conflict between a narrator and an employer over how bread should be made.

questions.stem: According to the passage, how does Mrs. Dalca decide whether dough is ready?

choices.A: She checks how long it has been rising on the wall clock.
choices.B: She presses a floured finger into it and watches how the dent fills in.
choices.C: She weighs it on the scale to see whether it has grown heavier.
choices.D: She tastes a small piece of it before shaping the loaves.

questions.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred that when Mrs. Dalca says "Taste what hurry tastes like" (paragraph 2), she intends to:

choices.A: warn the narrator that working too slowly could cost the narrator the job.
choices.B: suggest that the oven, rather than the narrator, caused the flat loaves.
choices.C: let the narrator discover that rushing the work produces bread without flavor.
choices.D: show the narrator that the bakery's customers prefer pale, mild bread.

questions.subskill: Meaning of a phrase in context
questions.stem: As it is used in paragraph 1, the phrase "dressed for" most nearly means:
The very short third paragraph ("It tasted like nothing. That was the problem.") mainly serves to:

choices.A: introduce a disagreement between the narrator and Mrs. Dalca about the recipe.
choices.B: isolate the narrator's realization before the narrator reflects on a long-held habit of hurrying.
choices.C: signal a shift from the bakery to the narrator's experiences at school.
choices.D: suggest that the narrator thought Mrs. Dalca's bread was usually flavorless.

questions.stem: Based on paragraph 4, before working at the bakery the narrator most likely believed that:

choices.A: working at night was more productive than working during the day.
choices.B: being patient was the most important quality a student could have.
choices.C: tests were unfair to students who worked quickly.
choices.D: doing things quickly was a sign of being capable.

questions.stem: In paragraph 6, the comparison of the crusts' crackle to "distant rain" primarily helps convey:

choices.A: the narrator's worry that a storm might keep customers away.
choices.B: the narrator's sadness as the summer job comes to an end.
choices.C: how faint and subtle the sounds are that the narrator has learned to notice.
choices.D: that the bakery's ovens are loud enough to drown out the weather.

questions.subskill: Connecting the ending to earlier events
questions.stem: Mrs. Dalca's final remark, "Now it tastes like time," most directly recalls which earlier moment in the passage?

choices.A: Her comment during the first week, "Taste what hurry tastes like."
choices.B: Her statement, when hiring the narrator, that the work began at midnight.
choices.C: The narrator's memory of finishing tests before other students.
choices.D: The narrator's noticing the smell of a strong starter.

questions.stem: The main purpose of Passage A is to:

choices.A: compare the construction costs of pipes and restored streams in detail.
choices.B: explain the engineering steps a city must take to restore a buried stream.
choices.C: argue that daylighting buried streams can bring ecological, practical, and social benefits despite its costs.
choices.D: criticize earlier generations of city officials for burying streams.

questions.stem: In Passage A, the statement that daylighting "does not merely decorate a city" primarily serves to:

choices.A: stress that daylighting provides practical flood protection in addition to its visual appeal.
choices.B: concede that daylighting's main value is how it improves a city's appearance.
choices.C: dismiss the ecological argument for daylighting as less important than appearance.
choices.D: suggest that most cities daylight streams for decorative reasons.

questions.stem: The author of Passage A suggests that the increased public use of areas around restored streams was:

choices.A: the main reason most cities decided to daylight their streams.
choices.B: limited to neighborhoods where no buildings stood above the old stream.
choices.C: a direct result of reduced flooding in those neighborhoods.
choices.D: an outcome that the projects' designers had not anticipated.

questions.stem: In Passage B, the author's central concern about daylighting is that it:

choices.A: always costs more than repairing the existing pipes.
choices.B: may be chosen for its appeal rather than for how well it manages water.
choices.C: inevitably harms the wildlife it is meant to support.
choices.D: is unpopular with the residents of the neighborhoods involved.

questions.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
questions.stem: As it is used in Passage B, the word "sobering" most nearly means:
According to Passage B, which of the following could limit the ecological benefits of a daylighted stream?

choices.A: The width of the restored channel
choices.B: The number of people who visit the stream
choices.C: Polluted runoff from the surrounding streets
choices.D: The installation of rain gardens on nearby blocks

questions.stem: Unlike the author of Passage A, the author of Passage B:

choices.A: frames the argument from the perspective of someone responsible for deciding how a city spends its money.
choices.B: acknowledges that daylighting can be expensive.
choices.D: mentions the wildlife that a restored stream can support.

questions.stem: Mrs. Dalca's statement "I don't know how long. I know what ready looks like" (paragraph 5) most strongly suggests that she:

choices.A: is reluctant to share her methods with a new employee.
choices.B: judges the dough by its observable condition rather than by elapsed time.
choices.C: never measures any ingredients when she bakes.
choices.D: privately relies on the wall clock but does not admit it.
